## What the model says

The EZ diffusion model ([Wagenmakers et al., 2007](https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03194023)) is the diffusion
model ([Ratcliff, 1978](https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.85.2.59)) fitted to summary statistics instead
of single trials. Evidence starts between two boundaries, drifts at rate `drift` with noise, and the
response is made when it first reaches the upper boundary at `bound` or the lower one at 0; the response
time adds the non-decision time `ndt`. The diffusion model predicts three statistics in closed form: the
probability of an upper response, and the mean and variance of the response time. With the noise `s`
fixed at 1 and the start halfway between the boundaries (version `3par`), and writing $v$ = `drift`,
$a$ = `bound` and $y = -va$,

$$
P(\text{upper}) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{y}}, \qquad
\text{MRT} = \texttt{ndt} + \frac{a}{2v}\,\frac{1 - e^{y}}{1 + e^{y}}, \qquad
\text{VRT} = \frac{a}{2v^3}\,\frac{2y e^{y} - e^{2y} + 1}{(e^{y} + 1)^2}.
$$

At `drift` = 0 the two fractions are 0/0, and their limits are $a^2/4$ for the mean decision time and
$a^4/24$ for its variance; bmm switches to a series near zero drift, and so does this page. The
non-decision time adds to the mean and not to the variance; what remains of the response time is the
decision time. With the start halfway, the decision
time has the same distribution whichever boundary is reached, so `3par` uses the mean and variance of
all response times together. Version `4par` lets the start, `zr` × `bound`, move; then the two responses
differ in their decision times, and the model uses the mean and variance of each response separately
([Srivastava et al., 2016](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmp.2016.10.001)).

## The task

One trial is a choice between two responses, with the response time recorded. The model never sees the
trials: it takes, for each cell of the design (a participant in a condition), the number of trials
`n_trials`, the number of upper responses `n_upper`, and the mean `mean_rt` and variance `var_rt` of the
response times, in seconds. [`ezdm_summary_stats()`](https://venpopov.com/bmm/articles/bmm_ezdm.html) computes them from
trial-level data. The task panel
draws five evidence paths from the start under the current parameters, with the noise of each path held
fixed while the sliders move; blue paths end at the upper boundary, orange ones at the lower. The paths
illustrate the process; the statistics are computed from the formulas, not from them.

## Explore

The panel *Predicted summary statistics* is the forward EZ map: the summary statistics the current
parameters predict. The bar is P(upper), the probability of response 1. Below it is one row of response
times in `3par` and one per response in `4par`: the grey part is `ndt`, the coloured part the mean
decision time, and the whiskers one standard deviation (the square root of VRT) either side of the mean
response time; where the SD exceeds the mean, the left whisker stops at 0 s. Moving `drift` away from 0 makes one response more likely (positive: the upper) and shortens and narrows
the response times. Raising `bound` makes the
responses slower and more variable and, for a drift other than 0, more often the one the drift favours.
`ndt` shifts the mean and leaves the SD alone. In `4par`, moving `zr` toward 1 makes upper responses more
frequent and faster and lower responses slower.

Slider ranges come from bmm's default priors for `ezdm()`. `bound` is estimated on the log scale with a
normal(0, 0.5) prior, `ndt` on the log scale with normal(−1.5, 0.5), and `zr` on the logit scale with
normal(0, 0.5); each slider spans the prior mean ± 3 SD: `bound` from 0.22 to 4.48, `ndt` from 0.05 to
1 s, `zr` from 0.18 to 0.82. `drift` has an identity link and a cauchy(0, 1) prior, which has no standard
deviation; its slider spans the location ± 3 scale, from −3 to 3. The sliders start at the prior means
(dashed): `drift` = 0, `bound` = 1, `ndt` = 0.22 s, `zr` = 0.5. With no drift and the start in the middle,
both responses are equally likely.

## Across task settings

The predicted statistics do not depend on `n_trials`, but the likelihood does. The statistics of one cell
are themselves data, and `dezdm()` scores them against how much they would vary from one sample of
`n_trials` trials to the next ([Chávez De la Peña & Vandekerckhove,
2025](https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-025-02729-y)). The number of upper responses is binomial. The
observed variance follows a gamma distribution with mean VRT; its sampling variance adds the fourth
cumulant of the decision time, divided by the number of trials (in `4par`, those at that boundary), to
the term a normal sample would have. The observed mean, given the observed variance, follows a normal
distribution, and the third cumulant, divided by the same number, is the covariance of the two, so the
mean of that normal shifts with the observed variance. The panel *Across trial counts* shows the result: ±2 standard deviations of the
observed P(upper) and of the observed mean response time around the prediction. Both bands narrow with
the square root of `n_trials`, so a cell with more trials pins the parameters down more tightly. In
`4par`, each response's mean comes from the trials that ended at that boundary only (the panel uses
the expected count, `n_trials` × P(upper) or its complement), so a rare response has a wide band.
A boundary reached fewer than twice has no variance; `dezdm()` then drops that boundary's response-time
terms and keeps the binomial term for `n_upper` and, if the other boundary has at least 2 responses, the
other boundary's response-time terms. A response's band therefore starts at the first `n_trials` for which the call in *In bmm* has at least 2
responses at that boundary. That call rounds the expected count of upper responses to give `n_upper` and
leaves `n_trials` − `n_upper` for the lower, so the band starts at an expected count of about 1.5.

## In bmm

```{=html}
<div class="ex-widget">
  <pre class="ex-code" id="ezdm-code"></pre>
  <button type="button" class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-secondary" id="ezdm-copy">Copy</button>
</div>
<script type="module" src="../js/pages/ezdm.js"></script>
```

The code updates with the controls. `ezdm()` defines the model from the names of the columns that hold
the summary statistics (two names each for `mean_rt` and `var_rt` in `4par`: upper, then lower).
`dezdm()` returns the log likelihood of one cell's statistics; the call here passes the statistics the
current parameters predict for `n_trials` trials, rounded as shown, and the comment under it holds the
value this page computes for them. `bmf()` writes the formula for `bmm()`, which estimates the parameters
from one row per cell; `my_data` stands for your own data, and fitting runs Stan through brms. See the
[EZ diffusion article](https://venpopov.com/bmm/articles/bmm_ezdm.html) for the sampling model and for
`ezdm_summary_stats()`, and the reference pages for
[`ezdm()`](https://venpopov.com/bmm/reference/ezdm.html) and
[`dezdm()`](https://venpopov.com/bmm/reference/ezdm_dist.html).
